stories.title: Why We Built a Chatbot at All
stories.situation: Before we had a chatbot, customers could only reach CheapOair support through call or email. Around 60% of our bookings are international with respect to the US, so calling in was expensive for customers because of roaming charges, and email didn't get them quick support.
stories.task: I needed to figure out whether a new support channel was actually justified, and which one, before pushing for the investment.
stories.action: I ran surveys to understand customers' preferred channel for support, pulled customer feedback on our IVR, and gathered feedback from Operations agents who were conveying the voice of the customer from the front line. I used all three inputs together to build the case.
stories.result: Those three inputs pointed to the same conclusion, so we launched a chatbot for quick support for flight post-booking queries, starting with basic flows like booking details and billing details, and handing off anything more complex to travel experts.
stories.sourceQuote: 60% of bookings are international (wrt US),  so calling was expensive as well due to roaming and email doesn’t get quick support.

stories.title: Scaling the Dialogflow ES Chatbot from 20% to 50% Automation
stories.situation: When we first launched the chatbot, it only had 20% automation, meaning that fraction of queries were resolved end-to-end by the bot itself. We had onboarded basic flows like booking details and billing details, and anything transactional or needing extra support was handed off to travel experts.
stories.task: My job was to grow that automation percentage by onboarding more self-serve flows without hurting the experience.
stories.action: The chatbot was built on Google's Dialogflow ES, where I had to define each intent manually by adding the training phrases that denoted that intent, since Dialogflow ES uses NLP keyword matching between the typed query and the training phrases. For each intent I defined the response, the CTAs, and the sub-intents so users could converse through a flow. I onboarded self-serve flows for new bookings, cancellations, exchanges, schedule changes, add-ons, CCD, and CCV. I coordinated with different product and business owners to understand each process, then supervised the end-to-end integrations, and onboarded different agent teams to back the chatbot for anything it couldn't resolve. Day to day, I reviewed chat transcripts, stayed connected with stakeholders, and pulled insights from feedback to shape the next set of improvements to the chat experience.
stories.result: We took the chatbot to 50% automation, with 62% CSAT and 60% engagement.
stories.sourceQuote: On DF chatbot afterwards, we achieved 50% automation with 62% CSAT. Engagement 60% this is through onboarding self-serve flows like new bookings, cancellations, exchanges, schedule changes, add-ons, ccd, ccv.

stories.title: Blocking the Typing Box to Stop Intent Drift
stories.situation: About three years in, gen-AI chatbots became the norm and customers started typing freely into our chatbot the way they would on ChatGPT. That exposed the real limitation of Dialogflow ES: it's a basic NLP engine that can't handle multi-turn conversation, free-flow casual conversation, or context. Users' intent wasn't being classified properly, so the wrong flow would run.
stories.task: I had to stop users from getting derailed mid-flow on our highest-value journeys, since it was costing us both conversion and satisfaction.
stories.action: On the major flows -- exchange, cancel, schedule change and add-ons -- once intent was identified from CTAs or the booking source, I locked the typing box so users moved through the defined path. Ops objected that struggling customers couldn't reach an expert, so I mapped every step where questions arise and added a 'chat with an expert' fallback at each one, turning their objection into a requirement.
stories.result: Revenue rose, CSAT stayed flat, and there were no complaints about the locked box.
stories.sourceQuote: we have taken strategic decision for the major flows (exch, cancel, schedule, add-ons) once intent is identified from CTAs or based on source of booking, we block the typing box and let user flow the fixed defined path

stories.title: Killing the Dialogflow CX Migration on Cost and ROI
stories.situation: In parallel with fixing intent drift on Dialogflow ES, we started a proof of concept on Dialogflow CX, Google's version with Gen AI capabilities. We connected directly with Google's POC team and had multiple sessions to understand the product, how to use it, and what benefits it offered. They walked us through the complete architecture, including webhook handling, and the upgraded interface made it look like a straightforward migration from the lower version to the higher one.
stories.task: Decide whether migrating to Dialogflow CX was the right call. CX handled the backend for us but cost about 10x more and didn't fit the AI committee's annual budget.
stories.action: I reframed the goal: our problem wasn't architecture, it was customers not being understood. With that lens I put a cost/ROI comparison in front of the VPs of Product and Tech.
stories.result: CX was dropped. We built our own orchestration on Vertex AI (smoother since we already had the billing account), and it beat Dialogflow ES on every metric -- CSAT went from 62% to 80%. Lesson: decide what problem you're buying a solution for before comparing vendors.
stories.sourceQuote: But it didn’t worked due to the higher cost and ROI.

stories.title: Building the In-House Orchestrator and AI Agent Architecture on Vertex
stories.situation: After killing the Dialogflow CX migration, we still needed to solve the same underlying problem: weak intent classification and a limited chat experience on our existing Dialogflow ES bot.
stories.task: My main motivation was to build our own architecture on Google's Vertex APIs that would meaningfully improve intent classification and the overall chat experience.
stories.action: I drove the build of an orchestrator agent, which decides what to do with a customer's query, along with a set of specialized AI agents with clearly defined jobs: an Intent Classifier, a Booking Details Query agent, a Small Talk agent, an FAQ agent, and an Agent Summarization agent. On top of that architecture, we built five specific functionalities: Digression, which lets the bot continue the previous flow after answering an in-between query; Flow Switch, which asks for confirmation before transferring the user from one major intent to another; Flow Queries, which answers side questions raised mid-flow, for example mid-cancellation, and then resumes the previous step; Global Queries, which answers a query upfront regardless of where the user is; and Clarification, which asks a follow-up when a query is ambiguous and shows the possible next steps.
stories.result: Against the old Dialogflow ES chatbot, the new AI chatbot moved engagement from 58% to 70%, containment from 48% to 53%, and CSAT from 62% to 80%. The biggest ongoing challenge was mastering prompt engineering.
stories.sourceQuote: Created orchestrator agent (which will decide what to do with the customer’s query) and different Ai agents whose job was defined (Intent Classifier, Booking details query, Small talk, FAQs, Agent Summarization)

stories.title: Building the Offline/Online Eval System for the AI Chatbot
stories.situation: As we moved to an LLM-based chatbot on Vertex, we couldn't just ship it and trust it -- we needed a way to prove it was accurate and safe, and that it wasn't regressing with every change.
stories.task: I had to put in place an evaluation framework that covered the bot both offline, before release, and online, in production.
stories.action: For offline eval, we built test suites the chatbot was run against: golden sets for ground truth, adversarial sets for edge cases and prompt injections, and regression sets for basic testing. For online eval, we used an LLM-as-judge approach on top of app insights logging, tracking metrics for groundedness, faithfulness, safety, jailbreak resistance, and answer relevancy.
stories.result: This eval system gave us the confidence to take the chatbot through compliance review and into the phased rollout that followed.
stories.sourceQuote: Groundness, Faithfulness, Safety, Jail break, Answer Relevancy

stories.title: Getting the AI Chatbot Through Legal, InfoSec, and the AI Committee
stories.situation: Before we could put an LLM-based chatbot in front of real customers, it had to clear compliance -- legal exposure, information security, and our internal Gen AI guidelines.
stories.task: I owned getting the chatbot through that compliance process and then rolling it out safely.
stories.action: I connected with Legal, InfoSec, and the AI committee to work through everything from a compliance point of view, and followed the Gen AI guidelines the committee had put in place. Rather than going straight to customers, I opened the bot first to internal stakeholders for testing, then to the whole org, circulating feedback forms and improving the bot based on the suggestions we got back.
stories.result: Once we'd resolved the internal feedback, we made the chatbot live for 5% of traffic as the first real customer-facing rollout step.
stories.sourceQuote: We first opened it for internal stakeholders for testing, and then to the whole org. Circulated feedback forms and improved on the suggestions received. Post resolving this, made it live for 5% traffic.

stories.title: From Sr. Business Analyst to Leading the Analytics Team
stories.situation: I joined Fareportal as a Sr. Business Analyst, leading the analytics team for Operations Product with one data analyst reporting to me.
stories.task: I was responsible for modernizing how the Operations Product org tracked and analyzed its own performance.
stories.action: I built out dashboarding and moved reporting from Excel to Power BI, automated the queries that fed the dashboards, and wrote extensive SQL to support the analysis. I did deep data analysis for the team, coordinated with all the PMs to review their requirements, analyzed whatever items had just been released, and helped with target setting.
stories.result: That analytics foundation, and the credibility it built with Operations leadership, is what led to my move into a Product role, starting with the Priority Leads project.
stories.sourceQuote: Started with Sr. Business analyst, where I was leading the analytics team of Operations Product, had one data analyst in my team.

stories.title: Priority Leads: Predicting Complaints Before They Happen
stories.situation: Moving into a Product role, I was given ownership of building a Priority Leads tool -- a rules-based system to flag customers likely to complain before they actually did.
stories.task: I needed to define the rules that would identify at-risk customers early enough for Ops to intervene, and make sure those rules actually got acted on.
stories.action: I defined the rules manually on Excel together with Operations leaders, coordinating with them daily. The rules came out of experience and out of finding loopholes in the existing system -- for example, prioritizing a user who had contacted us more than three times across different mediums like call, email, and chat. Once agreed, I had these rules built as SQL queries that controlled the backend of lead generation inside the CRM. Every rule carried an SLA, driven by the Ops leaders for their teams to close before it breached, and I kept monitoring progress through a dashboard of leads created and their status.
stories.result: The goal was to predict a future complaint and resolve it before it snowballed, and we reduced complaints by 12%. The process is fully automated today and still running.
stories.sourceQuote: we were able to reduce the complaints by 12%.

stories.title: Bringing Live Chat to the Flight Listing Page
stories.situation: After Priority Leads, I moved into building the chatbot from scratch, initially managing 4 developers and 1 QA with no dedicated dev manager. Two of my priorities were improving the experience for customers waiting in queue, and increasing engagement by predicting intent from where the user was coming from.
stories.task: I wanted to get customers booking help from a live travel expert directly on the flight listing page, without cannibalizing the online booking flow.
stories.action: I identified the specific triggers where a chat option should be tested, starting with low-conversion-rate triggers and expanding to idle customers, senior segments, multi-city searches, and no-results or sold-out cases. I set up rule-based routing so high-quality leads went to our highest-performing agents, while pushing Ops to review and coach the lower performers. To drive click-through, I experimented with several chat-icon UX variants -- tooltips, an unread-message counter, and an animated icon. I reviewed chat transcripts daily to find action items and improvement areas, and I integrated the chat seamlessly with OBE, the platform agents use to book flights: on a single click, the same search the customer ran online opened for the agent in OBE, and if the customer had already selected a flight to review, that same flight was highlighted for the agent, cutting agent handling time.
stories.result: The goal throughout was to add incremental bookings through chat rather than cannibalize online conversion, so I ran AB tests on every change to monitor that impact.
stories.sourceQuote: Seamless integration with OBE (where Agent book the flight) with the chat to reduce the AHT, on a single click - same search is getting opened on OBE to what customer have searched online.

stories.title: Search Explorer: A Bet I Shut Down
stories.situation: In Assisted Selling, many leads went cold after being transferred to an agent.
stories.task: Qualify leads before handoff so agents spent time on buyers.
stories.action: I built Search Explorer, which anticipated the user's next filter and showed value tiles like 'faster by 3hrs for $20 more'. When results came in, I compared absolute bookings, not just conversion rate: the old flow of a few questions and a handoff produced more total bookings.
stories.result: Users who finished Search Explorer converted at about 40%, but many dropped out inside it, so agents got about 5x fewer chats and net bookings fell. I shut it down and restored the old flow. Lesson: rate x volume -- optimising conversion rate can lose you bookings.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S9 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: Oli: Building the AI Trip Planner from Competitive Teardown to Phased Launch
stories.situation: Management asked for AI ideas; the strategic aim was an app-exclusive feature to drive downloads.
stories.task: I pitched an AI trip planner, later named Oli, and then had to turn the idea into a product that converts users into flight bookings.
stories.action: After the CXOs pointed the direction at flights, I kept discovery and itinerary as the path into flight booking. I started with a competitive teardown of Trip.com and MindTrip, documenting what they were doing well and where we could realistically leverage similar approaches. I circulated that analysis internally to get the product team's own take on how they'd plan a trip, and used that to find the pattern most people actually follow. I then spent about a month in working sessions with a UX designer to land on the right UI/UX, iterating repeatedly after reviews with leadership until we had the best version we could get to. In parallel, I wrote the PRD, deciding what would ship in phase 1 versus later phases, and ran daily meetings with the three development teams involved -- Chatbot, which owned the UI and chat functionality, RPA, which owned the backend generating the AI content, and App, which owned the surface Oli launched on -- to groom requirements and rework anything we'd missed. Oli's features spanned destination discovery narrowed by personalized info, day-wise itinerary planning, flight discovery as the ultimate conversion goal, hotel and car discovery pushed to phase 2, and full booking-funnel assistance with context across the listing, review, traveler-details, seat-selection, and payment pages, plus post-booking assistance linked back into our existing chatbot since pre- and post-booking data comes from different APIs. We tracked everything through AB test metrics, dashboards in Excel and Power BI, Google Analytics for the funnel, and app insights for logging. I launched it in phases -- internal UAT first, then org-wide exposure for feedback, then live to 5% of app traffic, then 20%, then 50%, then 100%.
stories.result: We launched in stages (internal UAT, org-wide test, then 5% → 20% → 50% → 100%), auditing transcripts and watching A/B metrics at each step to make sure we weren't cannibalising app conversion. Oli delivered +15% engagement and 65+ daily flight conversions, proven incremental by A/B tests at every stage.
stories.sourceQuote: Then first launched on 5% app traffic, then 20% -> 50% -> 100%.

stories.title: Launching WhatsApp Support via Meta APIs off Social Ads
stories.situation: I ran a survey on communication channel preference and found a significant number of users, especially in Asian and LatAm markets, preferred WhatsApp.
stories.task: I wanted to turn that preference into a new sales channel by connecting customers with travel experts over WhatsApp, sourced directly from social ads.
stories.action: We started by launching WhatsApp links embedded in Facebook and Instagram ads. I did the initial research into the full WhatsApp integration: the message types available on the Meta WhatsApp Cloud Platform, their costs, which template messages we'd need to create for our use case, what the dynamic greeting message would be per ad and flow, how the agent would know which ad a user came from so the value proposition matched, and the Agent-to-Booking-platform integration needed to cut agent handling time by passing search details and auto-opening the listing page for the agent, plus a flow to re-engage customers who went inactive. I ran a POC to figure out how a user on WhatsApp would connect to an agent on our NICE Max UI, and found the mechanism through backend polling. I then coordinated with the Marketing team on where to launch the ads and who should see them, and led the internal approvals for budget and Meta-billing setup.
stories.result: The objective from the start was to connect customers with travel experts to help them book, and we initiated WhatsApp support via Meta APIs on social media ads, generating 25 new bookings a day with $3.7K in daily revenue.
stories.sourceQuote: Initiated WhatsApp support via Meta APIs on social media ads; generating 25 new bookings with $3.7K daily revenue

stories.title: Cancel and Exchange Funnel RCAs and Optimizations
stories.situation: After we launched self-serve cancel and exchange flows on the chatbot -- flows that didn't exist before, when users had to call in or get transferred to an agent -- I tracked both funnels end to end. Cancel ran Entry > Cancel Intent > Cancel for some pax or all > Automated/Non-automated > Show refund details > Proceed with cancel > OTP > Success. Exchange ran Entry > Type of change > Search widget > Modify for some pax or all > Automated/Not automated > Show listings > Review page > Select payment method > OTP step > Success/Failure, with non-automated cases always going to agents.
stories.task: My job was to find where users were dropping out of each funnel and fix it.
stories.action: On the cancel funnel, I found a huge drop at the OTP step. I dug into whether users were even seeing the OTP box, whether they could type into it, whether the send button worked, and whether they were receiving the OTP emails at all or those emails were landing in spam, reviewing both the chats of dropping users and their feedback. Going into the API logs, I found the actual cause: the email API was broken for a few specific booking engines, so those booking types weren't getting the OTP email at all. Separately, on the exchange funnel, I found a drop from the listing step to the review step. I RCA'd it using data, logs, chat audits, and re-testing the flow itself; the data and logs didn't point anywhere on their own, so I checked whether a backend release had touched the listings, and it had: a release had added more airline engines to increase listing volume, which broke the cheapest/shortest/recommended sorting, so users were stuck seeing the same order regardless of their sort choice. I got that resolved with the backend team. Beyond the two RCAs, I also found two optimization opportunities: at the 'Show refund details' step in the cancel flow, users wanted to know upfront when they'd get their refund if they cancelled now, and were asking things like why they owed a cancellation fee if they already had travel insurance, so I had the UI answer those questions upfront. And on the exchange funnel's OTP step, since all OTPs at Fareportal went out by email only, we were getting complaints from users who couldn't access or find that email, so I pushed to add OTP via SMS, coordinating with the SMS team and the backend OTP API team to build the workflow within a sprint.
stories.result: After the backend release causing the sorting bug was resolved and the email API issue was fixed, both funnels returned to normal. The refund-details-upfront change increased the next-step transition by almost 15%, and OTP via SMS increased OTP-to-success by 8%.
stories.sourceQuote: Then from the logs of APIs, we got to figure it out the there is issue with the email API for few booking engines and these booking types were not getting the email at all.

stories.title: Launching Self-Serve Cancel and Exchange on the Chatbot
stories.situation: Before self-serve flows existed on the chatbot, users had to either call an agent or get transferred to an agent on chat to cancel or exchange a booking — there was no automation flow available.
stories.task: I wanted to automate cancel and exchange end to end on the chatbot, because the problem came directly from user feedback and because it would free agent bandwidth for tasks that could be automated.
stories.action: I started by understanding the automated APIs already backing the agent's platform and facilitated discussions with the API owners and the tech team. I wrote the PRD covering all the use cases and designed the user flow on the chatbot. For UI/UX I worked with the design team on mocks and reviewed them with leaders, iterating until we had the final experience. I groomed the requirement with tech, and after a few sprints QA tested it and, post UAT, we went live with an A/B test. Non-automated cases still go to agents — the chatbot only handles the automated ones. On exchange, 80% of cases are city/date changes, which is where the revenue lies.
stories.result: Once live, cancel converted at about 80 a day and exchange at about 50 a day.
stories.sourceQuote: Discovery of problems came from user feedback directly and want to reduce agent’s bandwidth for automated tasks.

stories.title: Adding OTP via SMS to Fix the Last Step of the Exchange Funnel
stories.situation: On the exchange funnel I saw room to improve between the OTP step and success. All OTPs at Fareportal went by email only, and we were getting complaints that some customers didn't have access or couldn't even find our email.
stories.task: I needed the OTP to reach customers another way, and that meant getting teams outside my own to make it happen.
stories.action: I started a discussion about sending the OTP by SMS as well. The SMS service already existed, but this was the first time it would be used for this purpose, so I coordinated with the SMS team and the backend API team that provides the OTP, created the workflow, and had OTP via SMS ready within a sprint.
stories.result: OTP to success increased by 8%.
stories.sourceQuote: Therefore, we started a discussion to give OTP via SMS as well.

stories.title: Answering Refund Questions Upfront on the Cancel Flow
stories.situation: Once the cancel flow was live I tracked the whole funnel and reviewed chats, and saw an opportunity at the 'Show refund details' step.
stories.task: Work out what users actually needed at that step and close the gap.
stories.action: Reading the chats, I saw users expected to know when they would receive the refund if they cancelled now, and some asked why they had to pay a cancellation fee when they already had travel insurance. I started giving those answers upfront through the UI/UX instead of leaving users to ask.
stories.result: It increased the next-step transition by almost 15%.
stories.sourceQuote: Tracking the funnel and reviewing chats, we see an opportunity at “Show refund details” step

stories.title: Building AI Agents to Turn Chat Transcripts and Complaints into Backlog Items
stories.situation: A big part of my day-to-day was reviewing chat transcripts and customer feedback to decide the next improvements to the chat experience.
stories.task: I wanted that review to be systematic rather than manual, so improvements kept flowing without depending on me reading everything.
stories.action: Using Copilot, I built two AI agents. One fetches chat transcripts weekly, analyzes them, and returns sentiment, key improvements and bugs. The other fetches all negative comments weekly, identifies the core themes, picks the top themes, runs through the comments, works out the key actions that could improve things, and auto-creates them on the Azure board.
stories.result: The weekly review of transcripts and negative feedback now runs as an agent workflow, and the resulting actions land on the Azure board automatically.
stories.sourceQuote: Build AI Agent to fetch chat transcripts on weekly basis, analyze and give the sentiment, keys of improvements, bugs.

stories.title: Asking for a Move into Product — and Earning a Bigger Product
stories.situation: I was leading analytics for Operations Product, supporting multiple PMs with analysis, dashboards and impact analysis, and I wanted to move into product.
stories.task: Get a real product to own and prove I could run it.
stories.action: I told my manager directly where I wanted to grow and explicitly asked for product. He gave me my first product, the Priority Leads Tool — Ops was maintaining priority cases in Excel. I coordinated with Ops leaders, turned their experience into priority rules and use cases, validated them with data, and worked with a developer to generate the leads in the CRM.
stories.result: The rules shipped, and the leaders gave my manager strong feedback on my thinking, which got me trusted with a bigger product — the early-stage Dialogflow chatbot.
stories.sourceQuote: Abhishek proactively told his manager where he wanted to grow — explicitly asked for product.

stories.title: Bridging US Leadership and the India Engineering Team
stories.situation: All our engineers were in India while leadership sat in the US.
stories.task: Make sure what US leadership wanted turned into specs the India engineering team could actually build.
stories.action: I acted as the bridge, translating US leadership requirements into specs for India engineering — across a team that grew from 2 developers and 1 QA to roughly 12 engineers, 3 QAs and 2 designers at its peak.
stories.result: This is how requirements flowed from US leadership to the India team throughout the chatbot and Oli work. (Add a concrete example here with the Edit button — a specific requirement you had to reshape.)
stories.sourceQuote: he was the bridge translating US leadership requirements into specs for India engineering

stories.title: Running the Chatbot Team with No Dev Manager
stories.situation: I was handed the Dialogflow chatbot at a very early stage with 2 developers and 1 QA and no dev manager.
stories.task: Run the team and the product with nobody in the dev-manager seat.
stories.action: I filled the dev-manager gap myself while owning the product. The team grew to 4 developers and 1 QA, then added 2 developers and a QA when we onboarded transactions like exchange and cancel, and at its peak was about 12 engineers, 3 QAs and 2 designers.
stories.result: The chatbot grew from scratch into a mature product with around 50% end-to-end automation.
stories.sourceQuote: handed the Dialogflow chatbot at a very early stage — 2 developers + 1 QA, no dev manager (he filled that gap).

stories.title: IROP: A Hurricane Flood with Fixed Agent Capacity
stories.situation: A US hurricane triggered mass flight cancellations. Panicked customers flooded chat, agent abandon rates hit 30-40%, and Ops leaders escalated hard.
stories.task: Protect the customers who most needed help with the agents we actually had.
stories.action: I got Ops leaders and supervisors on a call and reframed the problem from 'we need more agents' to 'who do we serve first?' Together we designed an IROP flag Ops can switch on: only travellers flying within 7 days reach an expert, and everyone else gets an honest soft-disconnect message plus an auto-created callback lead so nobody is simply dropped.
stories.result: Abandon rate fell to under 5%. Chat CSAT dipped, which was a conscious trade-off, but overall CSAT recovered through the callbacks and downstream complaints fell. Lesson: in a crisis, decide explicitly who you serve, and design a recovery path for everyone else.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S1 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: Winning Over Ops on the AI Chatbot
stories.situation: Ops feared the new AI chatbot would cut chat volume to agents, and with it their headcount, revenue targets and incentives.
stories.task: Get Ops to back the AI rollout instead of resisting it.
stories.action: I ran weekly calls with Ops and addressed the fear behind the objection, not just the objection. I showed them they were already receiving misrouted chats, that the transaction APIs weren't changing, and that they'd get fewer but better chats. I committed to starting at 5% of traffic, reviewing results with them, and fixing their issues before any scale-up.
stories.result: Revenue rose instead of falling. Transfers to agents fell 8% and non-revenue chats fell about 40%. Lesson: find the incentive behind a stakeholder's pushback and design for it.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S2 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: Saying 'Not Now' to US Leadership
stories.situation: US leadership wanted the chatbot extended to B2B clients in Phase 1. The bot was B2C end to end, so it meant about 2 months of 2 developers and would have delayed Oli's 5% → 20% ramp.
stories.task: Protect the roadmap without simply refusing a senior ask.
stories.action: I didn't say no outright. I laid out the trade-off in effort and in what would slip, and proposed that B2B Phase 1 launch on phone support while we measured real demand. My VP backed the proposal.
stories.result: Leadership agreed and B2B went onto the Phase 2 roadmap. Phase 1 clients did only 20-25 bookings a day, which phone support handled comfortably. Lesson: 'not now, and here's the data that tells us when' beats 'no'.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S3 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: Prompt Engineering with No In-House Experts
stories.situation: We were building our own multi-agent chatbot on Vertex AI, and nobody in the company had production prompt-engineering experience.
stories.task: Get the bot reliable enough on real customer traffic to replace Dialogflow ES.
stories.action: I worked through three failure modes. Ambiguity: the bot guessed an intent, so I added a rule to offer the candidate intents as options and proceed only after the customer chooses. Hallucinated booking details (swapped dates, wrong layovers): I gave the agents strict API response schemas and a 'never assume, say you don't know' instruction. Orchestrator overload: with 100+ intents it confused voluntary exchange with airline schedule change, so I moved to hierarchical routing -- a category agent first, then a specialist.
stories.result: These fixes fed directly into CSAT rising from 62% to 80%. Lesson: most LLM failures are design problems you can name and fix one by one.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S5 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: Holding the Line on Quality: The Gated AI Rollout
stories.situation: The plan for the AI chatbot was dated stage gates from 5% to 100% of traffic.
stories.task: Scale the rollout without letting a date push an unready model onto more customers.
stories.action: I refused to move to 20% until online evaluation was live, then held for weeks while Booking Details groundedness rose from 65-70% to its 95% threshold. For the move to 100%, I wrote the approval email to the CXOs using actual A/B cost and ROI at 50%: the AI bot against Dialogflow ES, with a clear jump in cancellations and exchanges completed.
stories.result: Approved to 100%. Lesson: dates are targets; thresholds are gates.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S6 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: Disagree and Commit: Mandatory Sign-In
stories.situation: Arpit, our Director, wanted the standard sign-in on the post-booking chatbot for consistency and compliance. I argued it would cut authentication and therefore self-serve revenue, using sign-in rates from other channels as evidence.
stories.task: Make my case with data, and then deliver whatever was decided.
stories.action: I was overruled, so I committed and built it. When authentication dropped, I didn't re-argue the decision; I reduced its cost with banners and an auto-opened sign-in pop-up.
stories.result: Authentication fell from about 85% to 70%, as predicted, and the optimisations clawed some of it back. Later, when a refund-fraud case surfaced, it proved sign-in was the right call to keep. Lesson: argue with data, commit fully, then reduce the cost of the decision.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S7 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: The Sign-In Launch That Broke in Production
stories.situation: Fraudsters were abusing booking ID + email verification to divert refunds, and Security mandated sign-in on the chatbot. The Profile team's SDK didn't fit the chatbot, so we built a native email + OTP flow.
stories.task: Ship the mandated sign-in without breaking post-booking support.
stories.action: On go-live, QA monitoring caught that sign-in was failing: a production-only dependency flag hadn't been enabled, and every post-booking query was blocked. I rolled back within hours, worked with the team on the full fix (it needed more than the flag), and re-released.
stories.result: Back live within about a day. Lesson: keep a production-config checklist for anything on a critical path -- owning a native build means owning its dependencies too.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S8 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: Cutting Queue Abandonment from 15% to 3-4%
stories.situation: After 'transferring you to an expert', the chat input box locked with no information, so about 15% of customers abandoned, assuming the bot was broken.
stories.task: Keep customers in the queue until an agent picked up.
stories.action: Using ideas from NICE, I A/B tested showing queue position vs. wait time vs. both; both won and cut abandonment to 7%. I then added a prompt every 2 minutes letting customers keep waiting or get a callback lead, plus a light add-on line during the wait.
stories.result: Abandonment fell from about 15% to 3-4%.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S10 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: Scoping Oli's MVP
stories.situation: In design reviews, leadership asked to launch Oli, our AI trip planner, on every booking-funnel page on day one.
stories.task: Keep the MVP small enough to ship and to tell us whether the core idea worked.
stories.action: I pushed back: a funnel-wide launch needed page-level data contracts and far more dev and test effort, and it would cloud whether the core idea worked. I proposed homepage discovery first.
stories.result: Leadership agreed, and the booking-funnel assistant shipped in the next phase.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S12 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: Being Wrong About Oli's Users
stories.situation: Oli was built on the hypothesis that users wanted destination discovery and itineraries.
stories.task: Find out what users actually needed once Oli was live.
stories.action: I read the data and transcripts. CheapOair users come to book; their real uncertainty is about which flight, not where to go. I re-prioritised the flight agent over discovery features.
stories.result: The roadmap moved to flight-led assistance; proactive nudges are next, expected to lift conversion by about 20%. Lesson: launch data beats your own hypothesis.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S14 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: Three Pods, One Broken Data Contract
stories.situation: Oli failed when launched from the payment page. The AI team's API expected every parameter to be present, even as null; the App team dropped missing ones, and the Chat layer passed them through unchanged.
stories.task: Find the root cause across three teams that each believed their part worked.
stories.action: I raised it in the joint standup, traced the failure to the parameter mismatch, and wrote one data-contract document that all three teams build against.
stories.result: The fix shipped, and no further breaks of that kind occurred.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S15 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: The Eval Caught What the Golden Set Missed
stories.situation: Oli had passed offline testing against our golden set and was live on a slice of traffic with online LLM-as-judge evaluation.
stories.task: Use production evaluation to catch what offline testing hadn't.
stories.action: Online eval surfaced three issues. Oli resisted explicit requests to hand off to an agent -- there were no golden cases for this, so I added them. Oli exposed a user's email ID in chat -- I held the release until it was fixed. Next-step CTAs looped back to the same set -- fixed.
stories.result: All three fixed before scaling further. Lesson: the golden set is a living artefact; production eval keeps it honest.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S16 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: Generic Seat Map Blocked for Six Months
stories.situation: Management asked for a fallback seat preference (window, aisle, sit together) as a paid ancillary. Development finished in 2 sprints.
stories.task: Get it live.
stories.action: Test transaction IDs couldn't be created in the test environments, so it couldn't be tested end to end. I chased the backend team, but the feature stayed blocked until they enabled test TIDs.
stories.result: It was blocked for about 6 months. Lesson: 'can we test this?' is now a question I answer before committing a timeline.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S17 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: Unblocking WhatsApp Billing
stories.situation: The WhatsApp channel needed a new corporate card for Meta billing. Finance and the vendor team each needed justification, the process didn't exist, and the request was sent back twice.
stories.task: Get billing set up so the channel could launch.
stories.action: I escalated to my VP and put Marketing, Finance, the vendor team and the VP on one call to walk through exactly where it was stuck.
stories.result: Resolved on that call, and the channel launched. Lesson: escalate with a specific blocker and every owner in the room.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank S18 (interview, Oct 2026)

stories.title: Customer First: The ClubMiles Principle
stories.situation: We wanted to pitch ClubMiles loyalty sign-up inside the chatbot, across pre- and post-booking flows.
stories.task: Grow loyalty sign-ups without hurting the customer's actual task.
stories.action: I set one principle: loyalty pitches must never block the primary task. A customer who came to cancel must be able to cancel, and pitches must not collide with app-download prompts. I prototyped the experience and presented it to my VP.
stories.result: The principle shaped where and when the pitch appears. Lesson: monetisation that blocks the task costs more trust than it earns.
stories.sourceQuote: Fareportal PM Journey doc, story bank Also usable: Customer first (interview, Oct 2026)
